questions.title: When do WHERE and HAVING filter a grouped query?
questions.answer: WHERE filters input rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregates have been calculated. Filter an order's status with WHERE and a customer's summed spending with HAVING. This describes logical query processing, not necessarily the database's physical execution order.

questions.title: How can a WHERE condition accidentally undo a LEFT JOIN?
questions.answer: A LEFT JOIN preserves unmatched left rows by filling right-side columns with NULL. A WHERE condition requiring a right-side value can reject those rows. Put a right-side matching condition in ON when unmatched left rows must remain.

questions.title: Why use IS NULL instead of equals NULL?
questions.answer: NULL represents an unknown or missing value, so ordinary equality with NULL does not evaluate to true. Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL to test it. A WHERE clause keeps only rows whose predicate evaluates to true, not unknown.

questions.title: How do COUNT(*) and COUNT(column) differ?
questions.answer: COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(column) counts rows where that expression is not NULL. After a LEFT JOIN, COUNT(right_table.id) can count actual matches while COUNT(*) also counts the preserved unmatched row.

questions.title: Why use EXISTS to test whether related rows exist?
questions.answer: EXISTS expresses a yes-or-no relationship without duplicating the outer row for every matching inner row. A join may need additional deduplication if several matches exist. Choose the form that expresses the intended result, then inspect the database's plan when performance matters.

questions.title: What are the tradeoffs of adding an index?
questions.answer: An appropriate index can reduce work for filtering, joining, or ordering, but it consumes storage and adds maintenance to writes. The optimizer may choose not to use it. Evaluate real query patterns and execution plans rather than indexing every column.

questions.title: How does a window function differ from GROUP BY?
questions.answer: GROUP BY normally reduces rows into one result per group. A window function computes over a related set while retaining individual rows. Use it for rankings or running totals when the report still needs each underlying row.

questions.title: How do ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK treat ties?
questions.answer: ROW_NUMBER assigns distinct row positions; include a stable tie-breaker when deterministic ordering matters. RANK gives ties the same rank and leaves gaps afterward. DENSE_RANK gives ties the same rank without gaps, which suits finding a second distinct value.

questions.title: Why group related writes in a transaction?
questions.answer: A transaction lets related changes commit together or roll back together. This prevents partially applied operations such as only one side of a transfer being saved. You still need constraints and suitable concurrency control; a transaction alone does not make every business invariant correct.

questions.title: Why must paginated queries have a deterministic ORDER BY?
questions.answer: Without an explicit order, row order is not guaranteed. Even an order on a nonunique timestamp needs a stable tie-breaker, such as an ID. For frequently changing or large datasets, consider keyset pagination and define how updates affect the cursor.

practices.title: Report customers with zero orders
practices.prompt: Using PostgreSQL, return every customer and their order count, including customers with no orders. Use the sample CTEs in the solution: Ada has two orders, Lin has one, and Sam has none. Sort by customer ID.
hints: Start with customers and LEFT JOIN orders.
Count the matched order ID rather than every joined row.
practices.solution: Preserve the customer side of the join and count only non-NULL order IDs. The CTE sample is self-contained and does not create or change tables.
practices.solutionCode:
WITH customers(id, name) AS (VALUES (1, 'Ada'), (2, 'Lin'), (3, 'Sam')),
orders(id, customer_id) AS (VALUES (101, 1), (102, 1), (103, 2))
SELECT c.id, c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY c.id;

practices.title: Find the second distinct salary per department
practices.prompt: Return all employees whose salary is the second highest distinct non-NULL salary within their department. Use PostgreSQL. Tied top salaries must not occupy both first and second place. Departments with only one distinct salary produce no rows. The sample solution should return employee IDs 3 and 5.
hints: Use DENSE_RANK rather than ROW_NUMBER for distinct salary levels.
checks: Tied highest salaries both receive rank 1.
NULL salaries do not enter the ranking.
practices.solution: Filter missing salaries before calculating dense ranks. Query the ranked result to keep the second distinct salary level, including ties at that level.

practices.title: Calculate daily paid revenue above a threshold
practices.prompt: Return each date whose paid-order revenue is at least 100. Exclude pending orders before aggregation. Use PostgreSQL and sort by date. In the sample, October 1 totals 120 and October 2 totals 100; October 3 must be omitted.
hints: Use WHERE for the paid status.
Use HAVING for the total-revenue threshold.
checks: Dates below the threshold are omitted.
The query returns one row per qualifying date.
practices.starterCode:
-- Given orders(order_date, status, amount):
SELECT order_date FROM orders;
practices.solution: Filter individual orders first, sum the remaining rows per date, then filter the grouped totals. Use numeric amounts for exact decimal arithmetic in this example.
practices.solutionCode:
WITH orders(order_date, status, amount) AS (
  VALUES (DATE '2026-10-01', 'paid', 80.00::numeric),
         (DATE '2026-10-01', 'paid', 40.00::numeric),
         (DATE '2026-10-01', 'pending', 500.00::numeric),
         (DATE '2026-10-02', 'paid', 100.00::numeric),
         (DATE '2026-10-03', 'paid', 20.00::numeric)
)
SELECT order_date, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
GROUP BY order_date
HAVING SUM(amount) >= 100
ORDER BY order_date;
